quote: the twelve-year-olds are loud and nobody makes them stop
why: reports nobody's reaction (no one intervening) as the evidence that the noise is tolerated/ordinary, the exact banned pattern of standing in for evidence rather than showing it
suggestion: cut the "nobody" clause and show a concrete detail instead, e.g. "the twelve-year-olds are loud, kicking a water bottle down the row of empty chairs"

quote: She knows where the good parking is and she knows Ruth's mother by name and she knows to bring a jacket because it's colder up here.
why: three "she knows" clauses are coordinated with "and" as equal grammatical weight instead of a hierarchy, exactly the chaining problem the rule targets
suggestion: She knows where the good parking is, knows Ruth's mother by name, and never forgets the jacket, because it's colder up here.

quote: with a paper cup of something
why: "something" is a vague placeholder standing in for a concrete, nameable detail, the flattening abstraction the rule bans
suggestion: name the drink: "with a paper cup of the lemonade from the folding table"

rule_name: Automatic-fail narrator constructions: trailing explanatory clause
why: the clause after the comma tells the reader how to read the gesture instead of letting the fussing action stand on its own, the trailing-clause defect

quote: which nobody expected at her age
why: tells the reader how to take the grandmother's appearance instead of stopping the sentence at the fact, the trailing tail the rule says to cut
suggestion: cut to: "Her grandmother came and sits in a chair at the end of a row and tells three separate teenagers that they seem like nice young people."

rule_name: Automatic-fail narrator constructions: pointing at the scene
quote: That's the strange part of the following weeks.
why: explicitly signals "pay attention to this" before the scene has delivered anything, the exact construction the rule says to delete
suggestion: cut the sentence and open directly with "Everything keeps running."

why: the preceding list (classes running, labs going, the bell on schedule) already shows the school's indifference; naming it "unbothered" explains the image just rendered
suggestion: cut the tail and end on the list itself: "...and the ninety-one of them are packing boxes in the middle of a school that keeps ringing its bell on schedule."

rule_name: Ration a Character's Verbal Tic to the Moments It Characterises
why: the narration's reflexive precise/hyperbolic count is applied to a peripheral detail of Dad's with no tie to anxiety, control, or dissociation, the tic used as authorial autopilot rather than characterization
suggestion: cut the count and use a concrete image instead: "Her dad fills a memory card and gets none of her face."

quote: He's the best fighter in the year by a wide margin
why: a bare ranking claim delivered in narration with no evidence (no bout, no score, no name of who he beat); superlatives in narration are an automatic fail, permitted only in dialogue
suggestion: He's beaten every upperclassman he's sparred since ninth grade.

rule_name: Automatic-fail narrator constructions: interiority of non-POV characters
quote: this seems to him the obvious use of that
why: attributes Sam's internal perspective directly; the book is close third on Chloe only, and Sam is not the POV character
suggestion: replace with an observable action: "He signs the papers the way he laces his boots, without checking twice."

quote: the same way a fast kid runs track
why: a freshly built comparison delivered in the narrator's own voice rather than a stock/inherited figure or a line owned by a character
suggestion: cut the simile, or give it to Sam directly: "Fast kid runs track," Sam says.

why: this untagged line sits inside a four-turn exchange carrying only one attribution total ("she says" on the first line), leaving the reader to count lines to know who is speaking
suggestion: "It is a cost," Kavi says, not looking up from his phone.

rule_name: Ration a Character's Verbal Tic to the Moments It Characterises
why: a second instance of the narrator's reflexive exact-count habit, applied here to Nadia's browser tabs with no connection to anxiety, control, or dissociation
suggestion: cut the count: "She's got tabs open across two screens."

quote: Nobody in the chat has a good answer
why: reports the group's absent response as proof the question is unanswered/exceptional, the exact "nobody" pattern standing in for evidence
suggestion: give one specific non-answer instead: "Eli says he'll look into it and doesn't."

quote: which several of them find genuinely confusing
why: tells the reader how to interpret Priya's trip instead of letting the concrete facts (a bag, a year, no work in it) carry the reading, the trailing-tail defect
suggestion: cut to: "Priya takes a year and goes to South America with a bag, because there's no work in it."

rule_name: Automatic-fail narrator constructions: obvious causal clause
why: states a self-evident, generic reason the reader does not need spelled out, the obvious-because-clause the rule marks for deletion
suggestion: cut it: "So she takes the state school, an hour from where she'll be living, and the plan for the next two years is: wait."
